import sys

def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    if not data:
        return
    pos = 0
    S = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    K = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    out_of = [int(data[pos + i]) for i in range(S)]; pos += S
    nxt = []
    for _ in range(S):
        nxt.append([int(data[pos + j]) for j in range(K)]); pos += K
    n = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    syms = [int(data[pos + i]) for i in range(n)]; pos += n

    states = [0]
    s = 0
    for c in syms:
        s = nxt[s][c]
        states.append(s)
    outs = [out_of[x] for x in states]

    first = None
    for i, o in enumerate(outs):
        if o == 1:
            first = i
            break

    print("states%s" % "".join(" %d" % x for x in states))
    print("outputs%s" % "".join(" %d" % x for x in outs))
    print("ones %d" % sum(1 for o in outs if o == 1))
    print("first-one %s" % ("none" if first is None else first))

main()

explanation:
## The entire simulation

```cpp
std::vector<int> states;
states.push_back(0);          // the state before any input
int s{ 0 };
for (each input symbol c)
{
    s = next[s][c];
    states.push_back(s);
}
```

Two lines in the loop. A table-driven machine has no `if` chain and no `switch`
over states - the behaviour is **data**, and the code that runs it does not
change when the machine does.

That is how real tools work. A Verilog `case` statement describing an FSM is
synthesised into exactly this: a register plus a lookup, where the "table" has
become a truth table in gates. And a parser generator emits a transition table
plus a twenty-line driver, for the same reason: the table can be generated,
checked and minimised, while a hand-written `switch` cannot.

## Why there are n+1 outputs

Pushing the initial state before the loop is not an off-by-one to be tolerated -
it is the machine's behaviour. A Moore output is the current state decoded, and
the machine is in state 0 before the first clock edge, so it has an output then.

In hardware terms: the state register comes out of reset holding 0, the output
logic is combinational, so `out` is valid as soon as reset releases - before any
input has been clocked in.

## Moore and Mealy, and the cycle of latency

| | Moore | Mealy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| output depends on | state only | state **and** current input |
| output count for n inputs | n + 1 | n |
| output is stable | for the whole clock period | changes when the input does |
| detects a pattern | one cycle **after** the last symbol | in the **same** cycle |
| typically needs | more states | fewer states |

The two-ones detector above is a Moore machine with three states, and it asserts
at index 3 - the cycle *after* the second 1 arrived. A Mealy version needs only
two states: from "saw one 1", an input of 1 produces output 1 immediately, with
no third state at all.

So Mealy is faster by a cycle and smaller. The catch is that its output is a
combinational function of the input, so it inherits the input's glitches and its
timing - the output cannot be used by anything that needs it stable, and a long
chain of Mealy machines accumulates combinational delay and limits the clock.

The practical rule in synchronous design: **use Moore outputs for anything
crossing a module boundary**, where the extra cycle buys you an output that is
registered, glitch-free and has a full clock period of slack. Reach for Mealy
inside a block when the cycle genuinely matters.

This is also why `first-one` is in the output. It measures detection latency,
which is exactly the quantity that differs between the two styles.

## Why the state is read, then written, and never both

```cpp
s = next[s][c];
```

The right-hand side uses the **old** state; the assignment installs the new one.
In hardware that separation is the flip-flop: the next-state logic reads what the
register currently holds, and the register only updates on the clock edge.

In Verilog, this is the whole `=` versus `<=` business:

```verilog
always @(posedge clk) begin
    state <= next_state;        // nonblocking: all registers update together
end

always @(posedge clk) begin
    state = next_state;         // blocking: a later line sees the NEW value
end
```

Nonblocking assignment (`<=`) computes every right-hand side first, then updates
every left-hand side - which is what real flip-flops do, all clocked by the same
edge. Blocking assignment (`=`) inside a clocked block makes the order of your
lines matter, so two registers in the same block can behave as if one was
updated before the other - which no hardware does, and which means the simulation
and the synthesised circuit disagree. That is the classic simulation/synthesis
mismatch, and it is the single most common Verilog bug.

In C++ the distinction is invisible because there is only one statement here. It
becomes visible the moment there are two registers:

```cpp
// WRONG if both are meant to be clocked on the same edge:
a = b;
b = old_a;        // b already changed... and what is old_a?

// RIGHT: compute both next values, then commit both
int na = b, nb = a;
a = na; b = nb;
```

Which is why the shift-register version of this problem exists as a separate
exercise.

## Reachability, and what the table does not tell you

The state list in the output shows which states the machine actually visited for
*this* input. A table can contain states that no input can reach - dead states,
usually left over from editing - and nothing in the simulation points them out.

Synthesis tools do notice, and will optimise an unreachable state away, which
can quietly change the number of flip-flops. Worth knowing because an FSM with
an unreachable "error" state is a common and harmless-looking mistake: the error
handling is there in the source and cannot ever run.

The opposite problem is worse. A state machine that can enter a state with no
path back to reset is stuck, and in real hardware this happens when a glitch or
a single-event upset puts the register into an encoding the designer never
intended. The defence is an explicit `default` arm sending any unexpected state
back to reset - and, in Verilog, a `full_case` directive is precisely the wrong
answer, because it tells the tool to assume the unexpected cannot happen.

## `first-one none` and the sentinel again

```cpp
long long first{ -1 };
...
if (first < 0) std::cout << "first-one none\n";
```

Index 0 is a legitimate answer - the hidden single-state machine with output 1
has `first-one 0` - so "no answer" cannot be represented by 0. `-1` works
because an index is never negative, which is the same reasoning, and the same
limitation, as the search problem. `std::optional<std::size_t>` is the honest
version.
